romania.title: Invenția românească, dezvoltată la Cluj, care cucerește Europa: coșul de gunoi care sortează singur deșeurile. Cum funcționează
romania.summary: Coșul de gunoi care sortează singur deșeurile - nu e scenariu de viitor, ci o invenție dezvoltată la Cluj-Napoca. Cu ajutorul inteligenței artificiale, dispozitivul recunoaște materialele și le sortează automat în doar trei secunde. Invenția românească a fost prezentantă la un târg de sustenabilitate din Paris și a primit o finanțare europeană de 1,6 milioane de euro. Producția în serie este estimată să înceapă în vara anului viitor.

medical.title: Females with autoimmune diseases 'less likely to be believed' than males and face longer diagnostic delays
medical.summary: Females with autoimmune diseases are significantly more likely than males to have their autoimmune disease misdiagnosed as a psychiatric or psychosomatic condition, according to a study of more than 6,600 patients.

medical.title: Menopause is marked by a body-wide physiological 'cliff,' study suggests
medical.summary: The final menstrual period is preceded by abrupt "cliff-like" biological changes across multiple body systems, some of which show early signs more than a decade beforehand, according to research published in Nature Medicine. The findings suggest that menopause-related physiological changes may occur over a shorter time frame than previously thought and advance our understanding of how early these changes can be detected.

medical.title: Cardiac rehabilitation programs not keeping up with global increases in cardiovascular disease
medical.summary: Despite the rising incidence of cardiovascular disease (CVD), along with evidence that cardiac rehabilitation programs improve outcomes for those living with CVD, availability of these programs has not increased worldwide in the past decade, according to a new study by York University researchers.

medical.title: Tiny robots speed medicine through body to the heart
medical.summary: Johns Hopkins University engineers have created robots the size of a pencil tip intended to travel through the body to deliver medicine to infections inside a beating heart.

medical.title: Benzodiazepine use in first trimester not associated with higher risk for major birth defects
medical.summary: A population-based cohort study found that pregnant people who used benzodiazepines during the first trimester were not at a substantially increased risk of having a baby with major birth defects. The rates of overall major congenital malformations were comparable between pregnancies exposed to benzodiazepines and those that were not, providing reassuring evidence about the safety of these medications in early pregnancy. The study is published in Annals of Internal Medicine.

medical.title: Shared signaling regulator may link liver and pancreas dysfunction in type 2 diabetes
medical.summary: Maintaining healthy blood glucose levels involves striking a balance between the glucose produced by the liver during fasting and the insulin released from pancreatic beta cells after meals. In type 2 diabetes, glucose production goes into overdrive while insulin secretion becomes insufficient, a multiorgan dysfunction that contributes to hyperglycemia, or high blood glucose levels.

medical.title: Liver and brain pathways drive distinct symptoms in a rare epilepsy model
medical.summary: A recent study from Johns Hopkins Medicine reveals that pathways in both the liver and brain contribute to different symptoms of the same rare inherited disorder.

medical.title: Stem cell–like tumor state may help identify high-risk small-cell lung cancer
medical.summary: Northwestern Medicine scientists have identified a stem-like state in small-cell lung cancer that distinguishes a group of patients with exceptionally poor outcomes following chemoimmunotherapy, according to a study published in Cell Reports Medicine.

medical.title: More active mitochondria may help chronic myeloid leukemia cells withstand treatment
medical.summary: Researchers in Adelaide and Singapore have uncovered new clues as to why some people with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) respond better to treatment than others, finding that mitochondrial function in cancer cells could be targeted to improve responses.

medical.title: Low levels of blood pressure protein may flag treatment-resistant psychosis
medical.summary: In a preliminary study using blood and spinal fluid samples from 200 people, Johns Hopkins Medicine researchers say they have evidence that a well-studied protein involved in blood pressure regulation may serve as a marker for—and perhaps play a role in—treatment-resistant schizophrenia and other psychoses.

medical.title: Drug combination that reduces oxygen levels in tissues improves Parkinson's symptoms in mice
medical.summary: In a new study, Broad Institute researchers report that two small-molecule chemicals that reduce oxygen delivery to cells improved symptoms of neurodegeneration in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. The scientists had previously found that excess oxygen in the brain is associated with neuronal death in Parkinson's—and that reducing the oxygen that mice breathe could help reverse symptoms.

medical.title: Study examines long-term mental health and alcohol use trajectories following disasters
medical.summary: A study of people who had been exposed to a disaster found different long-term patterns of alcohol use and mental health that were interrelated and influenced by individual differences and the type of disaster they experienced. The study, published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research, calls attention to the long-term mental and behavioral health challenges of people who have experienced disasters and the need for interventions tailored to their particular mental health profiles to prevent problem drinking.

medical.title: Empathy can help make maternity care safer—here's how
medical.summary: Poppy Russell lived for just 12 hours. She died in April 2021 at the Princess Royal Hospital in Telford after suffering a brain injury during birth. An inquest concluded that her death was preventable.

medical.title: Study offers new clues about how genetic risk for Alzheimer's affects brain immune cells
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory have found a new clue that may help explain why some people are more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease. It suggests that a protein linked to the disease can change how the brain's immune cells handle fat and trigger inflammation. Those changes could help explain how a well-known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's affects the brain.

medical.title: New research shows promise for treating hepatitis C in pregnancy
medical.summary: Researchers and clinicians at WashU Medicine are helping reshape how hepatitis C virus (HCV) is treated during pregnancy, with a new study showing that a commonly used antiviral regimen can be used safely and effectively in pregnant patients in real-world care.

medical.title: Blind people and experienced musicians distinguish pitches better, with less brain noise
medical.summary: Are people who have been blind for most of their lives better at hearing than sighted individuals? In a new study in JNeurosci, Woon Ju Park, from the Georgia Institute of Technology, and colleagues explored this question by comparing tone detection and pitch discrimination in people with and without sight.

medical.title: What is normal eating behavior? Age, sex and weight all play a role
medical.summary: A study based on data from nearly 9,000 people in northern Finland shows that eating behavior varies with age and differs between sexes and BMI categories. The findings suggest that there is no single threshold that can be used to define abnormal eating behavior for everyone.

medical.title: The bacteria on your tongue could be linked to your brainpower
medical.summary: Whether you're a quick or slow thinker depends on several factors, such as the efficiency of the brain's wiring and the amount of gray matter in specific control centers. But there may be another, rather surprising influence, and that's the bacteria in your mouth. Scientists have found an association between the mix of microbes on your tongue and how well the brain performs cognitive tasks as we age.

medical.title: Gaming disorder screening may overlook women who play to cope with stress
medical.summary: Playing more and more, struggling to cut back, or continuing to game despite its negative impact on everyday life can all be signs of gaming disorder. But what about women who play video games and may be overlooked by conventional diagnostic tools?

science.title: Gravity and quantum information linked through a derivation of Einstein's equations
science.summary: Recent research shows that gravity and quantum information are deeply connected and that the shape of spacetime can be traced back to the way information is stored in quantum fields.

science.title: New research traces the origins and human impact of Britain's largest medieval lead industry through ancient teeth
science.summary: The first definitive evidence of when post-Roman lead production began in one of Europe's largest medieval lead-producing regions, the Derbyshire Peak District in central England, has been uncovered by archaeologists after centuries of mining had erased much of the archaeological evidence. The work has been published in Antiquity.

science.title: Magnetic sculpting transforms single-source fields into predetermined shapes with mathematical precision
science.summary: Magnetic fields are invisible yet essential components in technologies ranging from MRI scanners and particle accelerators to atomic clocks and future quantum computers. Each of these applications requires magnetic fields with specific shapes and properties. Today, creating such tailored magnetic fields requires researchers and engineers to design specialized, carefully optimized magnets or large systems of coils for each individual application—a complex and resource-intensive process.

science.title: Bacterial antiviral defense suggests ancient link to human chromosome protection
science.summary: A new antiviral defense system discovered by Columbia scientists could be adapted in the future into a gene editor that slows down aging in our cells and improves cancer therapies. At the same time, the discovery also sheds light on an ancient event in evolution that may have helped set the stage for the emergence of higher organisms.

science.title: Chemical disorder gives new ceramic film magnetic properties for potential low-power electronics
science.summary: A material thinner than a human hair may foster faster computing devices that demand less energy and store more data, according to a multi-institutional team led by researchers in the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences.

science.title: From nonmagnetic to magnetic: A 2D semiconductor with electrically tunable magnetism
science.summary: Researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS), in collaboration with scientists from institutions in Switzerland, the Czech Republic and Germany, have demonstrated a way to introduce magnetism into an otherwise nonmagnetic two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor and subsequently control its magnetic properties using an electrical voltage. The findings, published in Science Advances, establish a new platform for investigating electrically controllable magnetism in atomically thin materials, with potential implications for future spintronic technologies.

science.title: Data-driven cricket ratings could reveal undervalued batters and bowlers through peer comparisons
science.summary: An analytical method could help high-level cricket franchises make more informed decisions about player recruitment, retention and team selection, according to research published in the International Journal of Services and Operations Management. The approach uses data envelopment analysis (DEA) to compare efficiency using multiple inputs and outputs. In the world of cricket, this means assessing players against their peers rather than relying on individual statistics.

science.title: Reinforced vertebrae allow plunge-diving seabirds to survive high-speed impact
science.summary: A northern gannet scans the sea for fish from 100 feet (30 meters) in the air. Upon seeing a school, it pitches its body into a nosedive, somehow breaking the surface at 70 miles per hour (113 kilometers per hour) without breaking its neck. This daring maneuver seems to defy the laws of nature, but it's standard hunting behavior for plunge-diving seabirds.

science.title: Global satellite data reveal widening recovery gap between urban and rural vegetation
science.summary: A global study has revealed a striking divergence in how urban and rural vegetation respond to climate stress. The study was led by Jin Wu from the School of Biological Sciences, Faculty of Science, and professor Yuyu Zhou from the Department of Geography, Faculty of Social Sciences, at The University of Hong Kong (HKU), with Dr. Zhengfei Guo as the first author.

science.title: Cholesterol-linked drug boosts gene-targeting potency in early findings
science.summary: Nucleic acid therapeutics, such as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), have emerged as promising platforms for treating a variety of previously hard-to-treat diseases, including neurological diseases.

science.title: Vapor-based method creates ultralight aerogels without conventional liquid-based chemistry
science.summary: Researchers at National Taiwan University (NTU), working across the College of Engineering, College of Medicine and National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH), have developed a new method for producing aerogels, introducing what they describe as the world's first purely gaseous-born aerogel fabrication platform. The study is published in Nature Communications.

science.title: High-speed microscopy captures sugar-building enzymes forming rigid pairs and flexible assemblies
science.summary: From a rigid molecular pair to flexible assemblies with moving domains, the enzymes that build sugar chains display strikingly different behaviors.

science.title: Baby tooth places macaques in northern Germany more than 300,000 years ago
science.summary: A research team from the Senckenberg Centre for Human Evolution and Palaeoenvironment at the University of Tübingen and Leiden University in the Netherlands has examined a tooth from the Schöningen archaeological site in Lower Saxony. The study was published in Quaternary Environments and Humans.

science.title: Water-based process turns wood industry byproduct into carbon nanofibers for sodium-ion batteries
science.summary: A new study led by researchers at the University of Limerick (UL) has identified a new battery material from a renewable wood industry byproduct that could help reduce reliance on scarce and expensive materials.

science.title: New light-emitting organic materials could enable deep-tissue bioimaging
science.summary: Researchers at the University of St Andrews have identified the first examples of a new class of advanced organic semiconductor materials that could one day be used as bioimaging agents, opening up new possibilities for deep-tissue imaging. The study, published in Nature Communications, was led by the Zysman-Colman group in the School of Chemistry at the University of St Andrews in collaboration with the Pal group at Durham University.

science.title: Tiny fossils reveal a missing chapter of ocean life after Snowball Earth
science.summary: A rare assemblage of micro- and macro-fossils found in a roadside outcrop in South China, featuring thin ribbons, branching shapes and a tiny balloon on a stalk, offers a glimpse of marine life after one of Earth's most extreme ice ages.

science.title: New study finds the staffing structure of an audit office improves outcomes
science.summary: Audit firms rely on partners to oversee audits and client relationships; managers to supervise teams and projects; and staff to perform much of the day-to-day work. The more audit partners and managers are involved in supervising and reviewing audit engagements, the better the audits tend to be, according to new research from the University at Buffalo School of Management.

science.title: Primordial helium further confirms our understanding of the Big Bang
science.summary: In the early moments of the big bang, two elements were forged: hydrogen and helium. Technically, the tiniest traces of light elements such as lithium were produced as well, but nothing of consequence. The early universe was about three parts hydrogen to one part helium. All the heavier elements, from the oxygen in your lungs to the iron in your blood, were created through astrophysical processes—fused in stars, formed in supernovae or scattered by the collisions of neutron stars. Even in the present cosmos, heavier elements are so cosmically rare that astronomers group them all as metals.

science.title: Escape rooms give health care students a safe place to get things wrong
science.summary: The buzzer goes off. Three occupational therapy students are convinced they have worked out what should happen to their patient next. They are wrong.

science.title: Elephants continue to shape the savanna even after death
science.summary: Elephants shape the African savanna. They consume huge amounts of forage, dig for water, topple trees and affect all the animals around them. So, what happens to their outsized presence after these iconic animals pass away?

science.title: High-speed video reveals how honey bee stingers keep pumping venom after detachment
science.summary: Australian scientists have used high-speed video to uncover the unique mechanism that allows a honey bee's stinger to continue to pump venom into its target even after it has separated from the bee's body.

science.title: Fijian bee genomics suggest 99% effective population decline since European colonization
science.summary: The decline of pollinator species due to habitat loss and pesticide use over recent decades has been a global concern. Pollinators like bees and butterflies support both wild plants and agricultural food production, but many species are threatened and remain poorly studied. It's estimated that bees, in particular, pollinate between 78% and 94% of all plant species.

science.title: Love in the ruins: The paradox of modern romance
science.summary: Ask young adults about love in this day and age, and their diagnosis is bleak: They live in an individualistic society, dating has been reduced to an algorithm, and a generation is afraid to commit.

science.title: NASA’s SpaceX CRS-35 Mission to Launch Health Research
science.summary: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration. This research supports astronaut health during long-duration missions through […]

environment.title: Brazilian ranchers block government officials from demarcating Indigenous land
environment.summary: Since Sept. 23, a group of rural producers has maintained a blockade on the road to the Paquiçamba Indigenous Land in the Volta Grande do Xingu region of Brazil’s Pará state. The blockade is supported by local politicians and aims to prevent government officials from physically demarcating the land traditionally occupied by the Juruna (Yudjá) […]

environment.title: The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
environment.summary: Enceladus may naturally separate and concentrate chemicals from its hidden ocean as droplets slowly freeze and shatter on their way into space. The process could explain Cassini’s puzzling ice-grain chemistry while giving future spacecraft a powerful advantage in searching for organic compounds and clues to life.

environment.title: Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
environment.summary: Scientists may have solved why the length of Earth’s day changes by a few milliseconds over decades. Subtle shifts in the inner core appear to tug on the mantle, revealing a surprisingly dynamic world thousands of kilometers beneath our feet.

environment.title: Scientists expected these Galápagos sea turtles to wander. They stayed put
environment.summary: Yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos surprised scientists by staying remarkably close to home instead of making the long journeys typically associated with sea turtles. Satellite tracking showed that none left the marine reserve during the study, revealing just how important the islands’ coastal habitats may be to their survival.

environment.title: Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
environment.summary: Scientists discovered two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, showing that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science. One lives in the threatened Komarnica Canyon, where a proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.

environment.title: A broken rib from the world’s largest T. rex hid a 66-million-year-old secret
environment.summary: A broken rib from Scotty, the largest known T. rex skeleton, contains an extraordinary fossilized network of blood vessels formed while the dinosaur was healing. Scientists used neutron and X-ray imaging to look inside the 66-million-year-old bone without damaging it, revealing details rarely preserved in fossils.

environment.title: These tropical trees breathe at night to survive drought
environment.summary: Some tropical trees have evolved a clever way to survive drought by taking in carbon dioxide at night, allowing them to keep their pores closed during the hot daytime and conserve water. By comparing three Clusia species, researchers discovered that this water-saving form of photosynthesis, known as CAM, did not arise through a single evolutionary change. Instead, ancient genome duplications followed by millions of years of genetic reshuffling produced strikingly different strategies, from strong CAM to stress-triggered and hybrid forms.

environment.title: Stonehenge’s 6-ton altar stone may have traveled from Scotland by glacier
environment.summary: Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone may have been carried from Scotland to Dogger Bank by glaciers before prehistoric people transported it hundreds of kilometers to Salisbury Plain. The possible multistage journey suggests remarkable organization and raises the possibility that the stone was valued long before it became part of Stonehenge.

environment.title: Scientists say a critical Atlantic Ocean current is weakening and the effects could be global
environment.summary: Scientists have found strong observational evidence that a key part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation has been weakening across a wide stretch of ocean for nearly two decades. The slowdown could eventually reshape weather patterns, rainfall, storms, winters, and coastal sea levels around the Atlantic.

mix_items.title: Invenția românească, dezvoltată la Cluj, care cucerește Europa: coșul de gunoi care sortează singur deșeurile. Cum funcționează
mix_items.summary: Coșul de gunoi care sortează singur deșeurile - nu e scenariu de viitor, ci o invenție dezvoltată la Cluj-Napoca. Cu ajutorul inteligenței artificiale, dispozitivul recunoaște materialele și le sortează automat în doar trei secunde. Invenția românească a fost prezentantă la un târg de sustenabilitate din Paris și a primit o finanțare europeană de 1,6 milioane de euro. Producția în serie este estimată să înceapă în vara anului viitor.

mix_items.summary: Noua campanie Primark de conștientizare a cancerului de sân evidențiază puterea experiențelor împărtășite și a sprijinului oferit persoanelor afectate de cancerul de sân. mix_items.title: Gravity and quantum information linked through a derivation of Einstein's equations
mix_items.summary: Recent research shows that gravity and quantum information are deeply connected and that the shape of spacetime can be traced back to the way information is stored in quantum fields.

mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea Alinei și cum sprijinul oferit de Fundația Inocenți a ajutat-o să își dezvolte încrederea în sine, abilitățile școlare și curajul de a reuși. mix_items.title: New research traces the origins and human impact of Britain's largest medieval lead industry through ancient teeth
mix_items.summary: The first definitive evidence of when post-Roman lead production began in one of Europe's largest medieval lead-producing regions, the Derbyshire Peak District in central England, has been uncovered by archaeologists after centuries of mining had erased much of the archaeological evidence. The work has been published in Antiquity.

mix_items.title: Magnetic sculpting transforms single-source fields into predetermined shapes with mathematical precision
mix_items.summary: Magnetic fields are invisible yet essential components in technologies ranging from MRI scanners and particle accelerators to atomic clocks and future quantum computers. Each of these applications requires magnetic fields with specific shapes and properties. Today, creating such tailored magnetic fields requires researchers and engineers to design specialized, carefully optimized magnets or large systems of coils for each individual application—a complex and resource-intensive process.

mix_items.title: Females with autoimmune diseases 'less likely to be believed' than males and face longer diagnostic delays
mix_items.summary: Females with autoimmune diseases are significantly more likely than males to have their autoimmune disease misdiagnosed as a psychiatric or psychosomatic condition, according to a study of more than 6,600 patients.

mix_items.title: Bacterial antiviral defense suggests ancient link to human chromosome protection
mix_items.summary: A new antiviral defense system discovered by Columbia scientists could be adapted in the future into a gene editor that slows down aging in our cells and improves cancer therapies. At the same time, the discovery also sheds light on an ancient event in evolution that may have helped set the stage for the emergence of higher organisms.

mix_items.title: Menopause is marked by a body-wide physiological 'cliff,' study suggests
mix_items.summary: The final menstrual period is preceded by abrupt "cliff-like" biological changes across multiple body systems, some of which show early signs more than a decade beforehand, according to research published in Nature Medicine. The findings suggest that menopause-related physiological changes may occur over a shorter time frame than previously thought and advance our understanding of how early these changes can be detected.

mix_items.title: Chemical disorder gives new ceramic film magnetic properties for potential low-power electronics
mix_items.summary: A material thinner than a human hair may foster faster computing devices that demand less energy and store more data, according to a multi-institutional team led by researchers in the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences.

mix_items.title: From nonmagnetic to magnetic: A 2D semiconductor with electrically tunable magnetism
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS), in collaboration with scientists from institutions in Switzerland, the Czech Republic and Germany, have demonstrated a way to introduce magnetism into an otherwise nonmagnetic two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor and subsequently control its magnetic properties using an electrical voltage. The findings, published in Science Advances, establish a new platform for investigating electrically controllable magnetism in atomically thin materials, with potential implications for future spintronic technologies.

mix_items.title: Data-driven cricket ratings could reveal undervalued batters and bowlers through peer comparisons
mix_items.summary: An analytical method could help high-level cricket franchises make more informed decisions about player recruitment, retention and team selection, according to research published in the International Journal of Services and Operations Management. The approach uses data envelopment analysis (DEA) to compare efficiency using multiple inputs and outputs. In the world of cricket, this means assessing players against their peers rather than relying on individual statistics.

mix_items.title: Cardiac rehabilitation programs not keeping up with global increases in cardiovascular disease
mix_items.summary: Despite the rising incidence of cardiovascular disease (CVD), along with evidence that cardiac rehabilitation programs improve outcomes for those living with CVD, availability of these programs has not increased worldwide in the past decade, according to a new study by York University researchers.

mix_items.title: Reinforced vertebrae allow plunge-diving seabirds to survive high-speed impact
mix_items.summary: A northern gannet scans the sea for fish from 100 feet (30 meters) in the air. Upon seeing a school, it pitches its body into a nosedive, somehow breaking the surface at 70 miles per hour (113 kilometers per hour) without breaking its neck. This daring maneuver seems to defy the laws of nature, but it's standard hunting behavior for plunge-diving seabirds.

mix_items.title: Global satellite data reveal widening recovery gap between urban and rural vegetation
mix_items.summary: A global study has revealed a striking divergence in how urban and rural vegetation respond to climate stress. The study was led by Jin Wu from the School of Biological Sciences, Faculty of Science, and professor Yuyu Zhou from the Department of Geography, Faculty of Social Sciences, at The University of Hong Kong (HKU), with Dr. Zhengfei Guo as the first author.

mix_items.title: Tiny robots speed medicine through body to the heart
mix_items.summary: Johns Hopkins University engineers have created robots the size of a pencil tip intended to travel through the body to deliver medicine to infections inside a beating heart.

mix_items.title: Benzodiazepine use in first trimester not associated with higher risk for major birth defects
mix_items.summary: A population-based cohort study found that pregnant people who used benzodiazepines during the first trimester were not at a substantially increased risk of having a baby with major birth defects. The rates of overall major congenital malformations were comparable between pregnancies exposed to benzodiazepines and those that were not, providing reassuring evidence about the safety of these medications in early pregnancy. The study is published in Annals of Internal Medicine.

mix_items.title: Cholesterol-linked drug boosts gene-targeting potency in early findings
mix_items.summary: Nucleic acid therapeutics, such as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), have emerged as promising platforms for treating a variety of previously hard-to-treat diseases, including neurological diseases.

mix_items.title: Vapor-based method creates ultralight aerogels without conventional liquid-based chemistry
mix_items.summary: Researchers at National Taiwan University (NTU), working across the College of Engineering, College of Medicine and National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH), have developed a new method for producing aerogels, introducing what they describe as the world's first purely gaseous-born aerogel fabrication platform. The study is published in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Shared signaling regulator may link liver and pancreas dysfunction in type 2 diabetes
mix_items.summary: Maintaining healthy blood glucose levels involves striking a balance between the glucose produced by the liver during fasting and the insulin released from pancreatic beta cells after meals. In type 2 diabetes, glucose production goes into overdrive while insulin secretion becomes insufficient, a multiorgan dysfunction that contributes to hyperglycemia, or high blood glucose levels.

mix_items.title: Liver and brain pathways drive distinct symptoms in a rare epilepsy model
mix_items.summary: A recent study from Johns Hopkins Medicine reveals that pathways in both the liver and brain contribute to different symptoms of the same rare inherited disorder.

mix_items.title: High-speed microscopy captures sugar-building enzymes forming rigid pairs and flexible assemblies
mix_items.summary: From a rigid molecular pair to flexible assemblies with moving domains, the enzymes that build sugar chains display strikingly different behaviors.

mix_items.title: Baby tooth places macaques in northern Germany more than 300,000 years ago
mix_items.summary: A research team from the Senckenberg Centre for Human Evolution and Palaeoenvironment at the University of Tübingen and Leiden University in the Netherlands has examined a tooth from the Schöningen archaeological site in Lower Saxony. The study was published in Quaternary Environments and Humans.

mix_items.title: Stem cell–like tumor state may help identify high-risk small-cell lung cancer
mix_items.summary: Northwestern Medicine scientists have identified a stem-like state in small-cell lung cancer that distinguishes a group of patients with exceptionally poor outcomes following chemoimmunotherapy, according to a study published in Cell Reports Medicine.

mix_items.title: More active mitochondria may help chronic myeloid leukemia cells withstand treatment
mix_items.summary: Researchers in Adelaide and Singapore have uncovered new clues as to why some people with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) respond better to treatment than others, finding that mitochondrial function in cancer cells could be targeted to improve responses.

mix_items.title: Water-based process turns wood industry byproduct into carbon nanofibers for sodium-ion batteries
mix_items.summary: A new study led by researchers at the University of Limerick (UL) has identified a new battery material from a renewable wood industry byproduct that could help reduce reliance on scarce and expensive materials.

mix_items.title: New light-emitting organic materials could enable deep-tissue bioimaging
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of St Andrews have identified the first examples of a new class of advanced organic semiconductor materials that could one day be used as bioimaging agents, opening up new possibilities for deep-tissue imaging. The study, published in Nature Communications, was led by the Zysman-Colman group in the School of Chemistry at the University of St Andrews in collaboration with the Pal group at Durham University.

mix_items.title: Tiny fossils reveal a missing chapter of ocean life after Snowball Earth
mix_items.summary: A rare assemblage of micro- and macro-fossils found in a roadside outcrop in South China, featuring thin ribbons, branching shapes and a tiny balloon on a stalk, offers a glimpse of marine life after one of Earth's most extreme ice ages.

mix_items.title: New study finds the staffing structure of an audit office improves outcomes
mix_items.summary: Audit firms rely on partners to oversee audits and client relationships; managers to supervise teams and projects; and staff to perform much of the day-to-day work. The more audit partners and managers are involved in supervising and reviewing audit engagements, the better the audits tend to be, according to new research from the University at Buffalo School of Management.

mix_items.title: Low levels of blood pressure protein may flag treatment-resistant psychosis
mix_items.summary: In a preliminary study using blood and spinal fluid samples from 200 people, Johns Hopkins Medicine researchers say they have evidence that a well-studied protein involved in blood pressure regulation may serve as a marker for—and perhaps play a role in—treatment-resistant schizophrenia and other psychoses.

mix_items.title: Drug combination that reduces oxygen levels in tissues improves Parkinson's symptoms in mice
mix_items.summary: In a new study, Broad Institute researchers report that two small-molecule chemicals that reduce oxygen delivery to cells improved symptoms of neurodegeneration in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. The scientists had previously found that excess oxygen in the brain is associated with neuronal death in Parkinson's—and that reducing the oxygen that mice breathe could help reverse symptoms.

mix_items.title: Primordial helium further confirms our understanding of the Big Bang
mix_items.summary: In the early moments of the big bang, two elements were forged: hydrogen and helium. Technically, the tiniest traces of light elements such as lithium were produced as well, but nothing of consequence. The early universe was about three parts hydrogen to one part helium. All the heavier elements, from the oxygen in your lungs to the iron in your blood, were created through astrophysical processes—fused in stars, formed in supernovae or scattered by the collisions of neutron stars. Even in the present cosmos, heavier elements are so cosmically rare that astronomers group them all as metals.

mix_items.title: Escape rooms give health care students a safe place to get things wrong
mix_items.summary: The buzzer goes off. Three occupational therapy students are convinced they have worked out what should happen to their patient next. They are wrong.

mix_items.title: Elephants continue to shape the savanna even after death
mix_items.summary: Elephants shape the African savanna. They consume huge amounts of forage, dig for water, topple trees and affect all the animals around them. So, what happens to their outsized presence after these iconic animals pass away?

mix_items.title: Study examines long-term mental health and alcohol use trajectories following disasters
mix_items.summary: A study of people who had been exposed to a disaster found different long-term patterns of alcohol use and mental health that were interrelated and influenced by individual differences and the type of disaster they experienced. The study, published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research, calls attention to the long-term mental and behavioral health challenges of people who have experienced disasters and the need for interventions tailored to their particular mental health profiles to prevent problem drinking.

mix_items.title: High-speed video reveals how honey bee stingers keep pumping venom after detachment
mix_items.summary: Australian scientists have used high-speed video to uncover the unique mechanism that allows a honey bee's stinger to continue to pump venom into its target even after it has separated from the bee's body.

mix_items.title: Empathy can help make maternity care safer—here's how
mix_items.summary: Poppy Russell lived for just 12 hours. She died in April 2021 at the Princess Royal Hospital in Telford after suffering a brain injury during birth. An inquest concluded that her death was preventable.

mix_items.title: Fijian bee genomics suggest 99% effective population decline since European colonization
mix_items.summary: The decline of pollinator species due to habitat loss and pesticide use over recent decades has been a global concern. Pollinators like bees and butterflies support both wild plants and agricultural food production, but many species are threatened and remain poorly studied. It's estimated that bees, in particular, pollinate between 78% and 94% of all plant species.

mix_items.title: Love in the ruins: The paradox of modern romance
mix_items.summary: Ask young adults about love in this day and age, and their diagnosis is bleak: They live in an individualistic society, dating has been reduced to an algorithm, and a generation is afraid to commit.

mix_items.title: Study offers new clues about how genetic risk for Alzheimer's affects brain immune cells
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory have found a new clue that may help explain why some people are more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease. It suggests that a protein linked to the disease can change how the brain's immune cells handle fat and trigger inflammation. Those changes could help explain how a well-known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's affects the brain.

mix_items.title: NASA’s SpaceX CRS-35 Mission to Launch Health Research
mix_items.summary: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration. This research supports astronaut health during long-duration missions through […]

mix_items.title: New research shows promise for treating hepatitis C in pregnancy
mix_items.summary: Researchers and clinicians at WashU Medicine are helping reshape how hepatitis C virus (HCV) is treated during pregnancy, with a new study showing that a commonly used antiviral regimen can be used safely and effectively in pregnant patients in real-world care.

mix_items.title: Blind people and experienced musicians distinguish pitches better, with less brain noise
mix_items.summary: Are people who have been blind for most of their lives better at hearing than sighted individuals? In a new study in JNeurosci, Woon Ju Park, from the Georgia Institute of Technology, and colleagues explored this question by comparing tone detection and pitch discrimination in people with and without sight.

mix_items.title: What is normal eating behavior? Age, sex and weight all play a role
mix_items.summary: A study based on data from nearly 9,000 people in northern Finland shows that eating behavior varies with age and differs between sexes and BMI categories. The findings suggest that there is no single threshold that can be used to define abnormal eating behavior for everyone.

mix_items.title: The bacteria on your tongue could be linked to your brainpower
mix_items.summary: Whether you're a quick or slow thinker depends on several factors, such as the efficiency of the brain's wiring and the amount of gray matter in specific control centers. But there may be another, rather surprising influence, and that's the bacteria in your mouth. Scientists have found an association between the mix of microbes on your tongue and how well the brain performs cognitive tasks as we age.

mix_items.title: Gaming disorder screening may overlook women who play to cope with stress
mix_items.summary: Playing more and more, struggling to cut back, or continuing to game despite its negative impact on everyday life can all be signs of gaming disorder. But what about women who play video games and may be overlooked by conventional diagnostic tools?

mix_items.title: Brazilian ranchers block government officials from demarcating Indigenous land
mix_items.summary: Since Sept. 23, a group of rural producers has maintained a blockade on the road to the Paquiçamba Indigenous Land in the Volta Grande do Xingu region of Brazil’s Pará state. The blockade is supported by local politicians and aims to prevent government officials from physically demarcating the land traditionally occupied by the Juruna (Yudjá) […]

mix_items.title: The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
mix_items.summary: Enceladus may naturally separate and concentrate chemicals from its hidden ocean as droplets slowly freeze and shatter on their way into space. The process could explain Cassini’s puzzling ice-grain chemistry while giving future spacecraft a powerful advantage in searching for organic compounds and clues to life.

mix_items.title: Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have solved why the length of Earth’s day changes by a few milliseconds over decades. Subtle shifts in the inner core appear to tug on the mantle, revealing a surprisingly dynamic world thousands of kilometers beneath our feet.

mix_items.title: Scientists expected these Galápagos sea turtles to wander. They stayed put
mix_items.summary: Yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos surprised scientists by staying remarkably close to home instead of making the long journeys typically associated with sea turtles. Satellite tracking showed that none left the marine reserve during the study, revealing just how important the islands’ coastal habitats may be to their survival.

mix_items.title: Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, showing that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science. One lives in the threatened Komarnica Canyon, where a proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.

mix_items.title: A broken rib from the world’s largest T. rex hid a 66-million-year-old secret
mix_items.summary: A broken rib from Scotty, the largest known T. rex skeleton, contains an extraordinary fossilized network of blood vessels formed while the dinosaur was healing. Scientists used neutron and X-ray imaging to look inside the 66-million-year-old bone without damaging it, revealing details rarely preserved in fossils.

mix_items.title: These tropical trees breathe at night to survive drought
mix_items.summary: Some tropical trees have evolved a clever way to survive drought by taking in carbon dioxide at night, allowing them to keep their pores closed during the hot daytime and conserve water. By comparing three Clusia species, researchers discovered that this water-saving form of photosynthesis, known as CAM, did not arise through a single evolutionary change. Instead, ancient genome duplications followed by millions of years of genetic reshuffling produced strikingly different strategies, from strong CAM to stress-triggered and hybrid forms.

mix_items.title: Stonehenge’s 6-ton altar stone may have traveled from Scotland by glacier
mix_items.summary: Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone may have been carried from Scotland to Dogger Bank by glaciers before prehistoric people transported it hundreds of kilometers to Salisbury Plain. The possible multistage journey suggests remarkable organization and raises the possibility that the stone was valued long before it became part of Stonehenge.

mix_items.title: Scientists say a critical Atlantic Ocean current is weakening and the effects could be global
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found strong observational evidence that a key part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation has been weakening across a wide stretch of ocean for nearly two decades. The slowdown could eventually reshape weather patterns, rainfall, storms, winters, and coastal sea levels around the Atlantic.
